scope.concept: To tell an increase from the usual level, the window has to include time before the increase began. A fixed start keeps that stretch in view while you investigate.
scope.narration: Rejections started rising at ${incident.onset_clock} (${incident.onset_ago}). Start the window well before then, so you can compare the rejections before the increase with those during it.
scope.reasoning: Only the time before the increase shows which rejections are normal. Without it, everyday rejections and the increase look the same.
scope.evidence: The histogram should show a quieter stretch, then the increase.

demonstration.narration: Rejections started rising at ${incident.onset_clock}. I'll start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}, well before that, so we can compare the usual level with the increase.
demonstration.evidence: The window now starts at ${incident.window_start_clock}, well before the increase at ${incident.onset_clock}. The stretch before the increase shows the usual level to compare with. The start is a fixed time, so it stays put while we work.

drifts.note: You started searching before setting the time window; this step is about choosing when to look.

hints: Only the time before the increase shows which rejections are normal, so start the window well before the rise.
Click the date box at the top of Discover and type a start date and time followed by “to now”.
Start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}: type “${incident.window_start_typed} to now”. Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: You filtered on the rejection reason ${action.value}. Check whether it's the one that increased, not one of the everyday reasons.

demonstration.narration: Now I'll turn the same pill around, so it keeps only that reason.
demonstration.reasoning: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning this one around swaps the everyday rejections for the increase itself, with no new filter to build.
demonstration.evidence: Only ${param.incident.reason} rejections remain, and the histogram shows none before ${incident.onset_clock}, so this reason is the increase. The pill reads ${param.incident.reason} again, without NOT. Next, we look for what these rejections have in common.

isolate.title: Turn the filter around to keep only that reason
isolate.narration: Now keep only the reason that increased. Click the NOT pill and choose Include results. The same filter then keeps that reason instead of leaving it out.
hints: Keep only the reason that increased, using the filter you already have.
Click the NOT pill to open its menu and choose Include results. (Deleting it and clicking the + next to the reason in its Top values works too.)
Turn the ${param.incident.reason} pill to Include results; Show me can do it for you.
isolate.concept: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning one around shows the other side of the same filter.
isolate.reasoning: One pill switches between the everyday rejections and the increase, so you compare the two views fairly.
isolate.evidence: Once the pill includes the reason, the histogram shows only those rejections, starting when the increase began.

inspect.title: Look for who these rejections share
inspect.concept: Field statistics counts the distinct values of every field at once. A field with one value across all these rejections is something they share.
inspect.narration: Switch from Documents to Field statistics. It counts the distinct values of each column for the rejections in view. Look for a column about who signed in (client, country or app version) with one value across all of them.
inspect.reasoning: The increase could come from one client, one country or one app version. Field statistics shows every field's distinct values at once, so you don't have to guess which one to check.
inspect.evidence: One field has a single value across every rejection in view.

demonstration.narration: I'll switch to Field statistics, which counts the distinct values of every field for these rejections.
demonstration.reasoning: Any field could set these rejections apart, so we scan them all instead of guessing one. A field with one value across every rejection is something they share, unless our own filters put that one value there.
demonstration.evidence: Every ${param.incident.reason} rejection has the same ${param.facet.field}, while ${param.facet.others} each have several values. event.outcome and authentication.rejection_reason show one value only because we filtered on them. Each .keyword row repeats the field above it. So the ${param.facet.noun} is what these rejections share. The ${param.facet.field} column shows which ${param.facet.noun} it is.

hints: Compare every field at once, rather than guessing which one matters.
Switch from Documents to Field statistics, above the results, and read the Distinct values column for client.application.name, client.geo.country_iso_code and user_agent.version.
Open Field statistics and read ${param.facet.field}'s distinct values; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: Keep only the rejected sign-ins
goal.concept: Start from the problem itself. With only the failed requests in view, the histogram and every field's Top values describe them, not all traffic.
goal.narration: The window holds every service's traffic. Keep only the failed requests: find the field that says whether each request succeeded, and click the + next to the value for failed requests. Then look at the histogram.
goal.reasoning: Successful requests from every service fill the window too. Keeping only the failed ones leaves the rejected sign-ins, so the histogram shows how they changed.
goal.evidence: A filter pill keeps only the failed requests, and the histogram shows the rejections rising.

demonstration.narration: I'll start from the problem itself and keep only the failed requests, with the + next to failure in event.outcome's Top values.
demonstration.reasoning: The window mixes the rejections with every service's successful requests. Keeping only the failures leaves the rejections on their own, so the histogram shows how they changed.
demonstration.evidence: Only failed requests remain, and they are all rejected sign-ins. The histogram shows a steady level of rejections, then a rise from ${incident.onset_clock}. Next, we look at what the rejections give as their reason.

hints: Start from the problem itself: look at the failed requests on their own.
Open event.outcome's Top values and click the + next to the value for failed requests. (A filter on http.response.status_code works too.)
Filter event.outcome for failure with the + in its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That keeps the ${action.value} requests. This step looks at the failed requests on their own.
You filtered on a rejection reason before looking at the rejections as a whole. Keep only the failed requests first.

goal.title: Look at the rejection reasons
goal.concept: A field's Top values show how often each value occurs. The most common reason is the most likely cause, so it's the one to check first.
goal.narration: In the sidebar, find the field that gives the reason for each rejection, and read its Top values. Which reason do most of the rejections give?
goal.reasoning: Guessing which reasons are normal would assume the answer. Top values show how often each reason really occurs.
goal.evidence: The field's Top values show one reason well ahead of the others: the most likely cause, and the one to check first.

demonstration.narration: I'll check the rejection reason's Top values to see which reason most of these rejections give.
demonstration.reasoning: Guessing which reasons are normal would assume the answer. Top values count every rejection in the window, so the next filter comes from the data.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row, ${param.incident.reason}, is the most common reason in the window, well ahead of the other reasons. That makes it the most likely cause of the increase, so we'll check it first. The next step leaves it out, to see whether the increase goes with it.

hints: Let the data show which rejection reason is most common, instead of assuming which ones are normal.
Open the authentication.rejection_reason field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).
Open authentication.rejection_reason and read its Top values; Show me can open the reference field.

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}. This step is about which rejection reason explains the increase.
You filtered before reading authentication.rejection_reason's Top values, so the filter rests on a guess.

goal.title: See the window without that reason
goal.concept: Filtering a value out shows everything else. Compare what's left before and during the increase: if it stays at the same level, it's the everyday background.
goal.narration: Look at the rejections without the most common reason. In the reason's Top values, click the − next to it. Then compare the histogram before and after the increase began.
goal.reasoning: If the increase goes with that reason, the rejections left over stay at the same level before and during the increase. That's the everyday background.
goal.evidence: A NOT filter pill leaves that reason out, and the histogram shows the rest at the same level before and during the increase.

demonstration.narration: I'll filter out the most common reason, then compare what's left before and after the increase began.
demonstration.reasoning: Some rejections happen every day. If the increase goes with this reason, what's left stays at the same level before the increase as during it.
demonstration.evidence: With ${param.incident.reason} left out, the rejections stay at the same low level before ${incident.onset_clock} as after it. What's left, ${param.everyday.0} and ${param.everyday.1}, is the everyday background, and the increase went with ${param.incident.reason}. The pill reads NOT ${param.incident.reason}.

hints: Look at the window without the reason that stood out, rather than at that reason alone.

Open authentication.rejection_reason's Top values and click the − next to the reason that stood out. That adds a NOT filter pill, a small box under the query bar that leaves the reason out. (Add filter with the operator ‘is not’ works too.)
Filter ${param.incident.reason} out with the − next to it in the Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That keeps only ${param.incident.reason}. This step looks at everything else first. Filter it out with the − instead; the next step turns the pill around.
You filtered on ${action.value}, one of the everyday reasons. This step leaves out the one that stood out in the Top values.

goal.title: Check that no one else has this rejection
goal.concept: A boolean query joins conditions with and, or and not. Asking for what shouldn't exist turns an empty result into evidence.
goal.narration: Now test whether anyone else has this rejection. Search for the unusual reason, and exclude the value these rejections share. If nothing matches, the increase comes only from there.
goal.reasoning: Field statistics counts what is in view. A query for the reason with the shared value left out asks directly whether the reason ever comes from anywhere else.
goal.evidence: The query finds nothing, so the reason occurs only with that value.

demonstration.narration: I'll search for this rejection reason with the shared value left out. I expect no results, which would show the increase comes only from there.
demonstration.reasoning: Field statistics counted one value for these rejections, and a query can ask the same thing directly: this reason, and not that value. No results means it never comes from anywhere else.
demonstration.evidence: No results: no ${param.incident.reason} rejection in this window comes from any ${param.facet.noun} other than ${param.facet.label}. So the increase comes only from there. ${truth.conclusion}

hints: Show that the reason never comes from anywhere else, rather than relying on a count.

In the query bar, join two conditions. The first is the rejection reason with its value. The second is not the value these rejections share. Put that value in quotes. Here, no results is the answer you want.
Type authentication.rejection_reason: ${param.incident.reason} and not ${param.facet.field}: "${param.facet.value}"; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That search found records, so it still includes the value these rejections share. Ask for the reason with every other value, with not before that condition.

checks.title: Time window
checks.detail: We started the time window well before the increase, so we could compare it with the usual level.

checks.title: The likely cause
checks.detail: We kept only the rejected sign-ins and found the reason that most of them gave.

checks.title: Everyday background
checks.detail: We left that reason out, and the other rejections stayed at the same level as before the increase, so the increase came from that reason.

checks.title: Who it affects
checks.detail: We compared every field of those rejections and found the ${param.facet.noun} they all share, and a search for the reason without it found nothing.

answer.evidence: The rejection reason's Top values and the histogram, with the reason left out and then kept, point to ${var.finding_phrase}. Field statistics and an empty boolean query tie it to ${truth.scope} alone.
